title: Two mandalas
hookLine: the womb-world and diamond-world mandalas, hung side by side

cards: A blindfold goes on. The young monk is led forward in the dim hall and handed a single flower. In front of him, laid out flat, is a great painted mandala, crowded with buddhas, though he can't see any of them.
He's told to let the flower go. It drops. Wherever it lands, that figure becomes his link to the whole teaching.
Kukai's own report home says that when he did this in China, his flower fell on the great Buddha at the center, and not once but twice, on two different mandalas. Those two are today's word.

teach.b: Here a mandala isn't a pretty pattern. It's a map of awakening, painted: buddhas and bodhisattvas set out in their places around a center.
In Shingon, the center of both is Mahavairocana, the great sun Buddha, called Dainichi in Japanese. One mandala is named for the womb.
At its heart is a lotus in bloom with Mahavairocana in the middle, and figures open out from it, court around court, like petals, like a family.

teach.h: THE WOMB WORLD: A LOTUS, COMPASSION.
teach.b: Shingon teachers link it with compassion, and with the way awakening is already present in all things, the way a child is held in a womb before it's born.
The other is named for the diamond, or thunderbolt, the thing that cannot be broken. It's laid out as a grid of squares, each square its own assembly of buddhas.

Shingon teachers link it with wisdom, sharp and unbreakable, the mind that sees clearly. In Shingon halls the two often hang facing each other, or on either side of the altar. And here is the point of the pair.

teach.h: THE DIAMOND WORLD: A GRID, WISDOM.
teach.b: Shingon teaches that they are two, and not two: compassion and wisdom, the world as it is and the mind that knows it.
Neither is the real one with the other as decoration.

A practitioner sits between them, in the middle, and practice is the work of letting the two meet. Some readers take Kukai's flower, falling on the center of each, as a sign that he would hold both together.

how: In Shingon temples the womb-world and diamond-world mandalas are commonly hung as a pair; in initiation, the student casts a flower onto a mandala to form a bond with a buddha, and practitioners meditate on both.

o: a pair of rival temples on two Japanese mountains
two paintings showing a heaven and a hell for the dead
Shingon's womb and diamond worlds, two and not two

games.q: the two mandalas: tap the pairs.
p: a lotus at the heart, compassion
the great sun Buddha at the center
a link to the whole teaching

s: in Shingon, one mandala is real and the other decoration
they're taught as two, and not two.
Kukai's report says his flower fell on the central Buddha
the diamond world is laid out as a lotus
the diamond world is a grid of squares. the womb world opens from a lotus.

games.q: blindfolded, you're handed a flower over a great mandala. what are you told to do?
o: let it fall where it falls.
keep it until the blindfold comes off.
games.why: wherever it lands, that figure becomes your link. Kukai's own report says his fell on the center, twice.

practice: Find a pair near you, your two hands, two windows, two shoes by the door, and let your eyes rest on one, then the other, noticing how each is different: shape, wear, which way it faces.
Then notice how they belong together, each making sense next to the other, and breathe with both in view.

wordCard.voice: Two mandalas. The womb world and the diamond world of Shingon, compassion and wisdom, hung side by side and taught as two and not two. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit garbhadhatu and vajradhatu: the womb realm and the diamond realm.

carryVoice: Your line: two worlds. Compassion and wisdom, two and not two, side by side. Until tomorrow.
